To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

transitional immature B cells have lower membrane cholesterol than mature B cells and that the relatively low membrane cholesterol content of transitional immature B cells is a major determinant of their impaired ability to compartmentalize and signal through their BCRs.

the membrane cholesterol content of transitional immature B cells is lower than mature-stage B cells, and that the lower membrane cholesterol content of immature B cells is responsible for the differences in the BCR compartmentalization and signaling that we observed between transitional immature and mature stage B cells.
immature B cells maintain lower levels of cholesterol than mature B cells and that this difference is important for the ability of immature B cells to tolerate self-reactive BCRs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of membrane lipids in the regulation of immune cell signaling.
the molecular mechanisms that underlie the development of B cells and their role in the immune system.
the molecular mechanisms that regulate B cell development, and in particular the mechanisms that control B cell receptor signaling.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cholesterol content in the plasma membrane is a critical factor for BCR signaling.
the cholesterol content in the plasma membrane is a key determinant for the BCR compartmentalization and the signaling capacity in immature B cells.
the BCR signaling is impaired in immature B cells because they have a low cholesterol content, and this is the main reason why these cells are tolerant to self-antigens.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the membrane cholesterol content of transitional immature B cells is significantly lower than that of mature-stage splenic follicular B cells.
cholesterol content is a key factor in determining the ability of BCR to form lipid raft domains and to sustain certain aspects.
cholesterol levels in B cell membranes are important for compartmentalization of the BCR and signaling.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the lipid composition of the plasma membrane can be developmentally regulated, and these differences can have functional consequences.
membrane cholesterol content can be used as a marker to distinguish between different B cell developmental stages and to identify differences in BCR signaling in these stages.
the cholesterol content of the plasma membrane is important in regulating the B cell receptor (a.k.a. the B cell antigen receptor) and its signaling.
